questions.q: Why is "public endpoint with a tight firewall" not the same security posture as "no public endpoint at all"?
options: The public, DNS-resolvable, internet-routable endpoint still exists and is a target for scanning and configuration drift, even if current rules are tight — a Private Endpoint removes that target for private-path traffic entirely
They are functionally identical in every scenario, just with different setup cost
A tight firewall is always stricter than a Private Endpoint
Firewall rules cannot be changed once configured, so drift is not a real risk
questions.explain: A firewall rule is a setting that can widen by mistake; the endpoint never stops being reachable from the internet the moment that happens.

questions.q: What is 'configuration drift' as described in this lesson, and why does it matter for a gated-public posture?
options: A rule or setting (like an accidentally widened IP range, or a leftover test rule) that increases exposure over time — and because the endpoint is public, that drift is reachable from the internet the instant it happens
A term describing normal, harmless clock skew between Azure regions
A feature of Private Endpoints that makes them less secure over time
A synonym for Transparent Data Encryption key rotation
questions.explain: Fully private connectivity removes the target itself, so there's no public listener to drift toward.

questions.q: According to the decision framework in this lesson, what should you check FIRST when deciding between a gated-public and a fully private posture?
options: Whether a compliance or contractual requirement explicitly requires no public network path — if so, a Private Endpoint isn't optional
Whether Always Encrypted is already configured
Whether the database has row-level security enabled
Whether the server is using SQL authentication or Entra ID
questions.explain: If compliance language demands no public path, that requirement overrides operational convenience arguments.

questions.q: What is a real operational cost of going fully private that this lesson calls out?
options: Every legitimate client needs network line-of-sight into the VNet (VPN, ExpressRoute, peering, or a jump box), and some SaaS/BI integrations may not support connecting that way at all
Fully private connectivity has no downsides in any scenario
It removes the need for any firewall configuration whatsoever
It automatically disables Transparent Data Encryption
questions.explain: Treating "always go fully private" as automatically correct ignores real client connectivity and integration constraints.

questions.q: Per this lesson, can a real environment reasonably use BOTH a Private Endpoint and a firewalled public path at the same time?
options: Yes — many real environments run a Private Endpoint for most production traffic while keeping a tightly firewalled path open for one legacy integration that can't yet reach the VNet
No — Azure SQL only allows exactly one connectivity posture at a time
No — enabling a Private Endpoint automatically disables all firewall rules permanently
Yes, but only if Dynamic Data Masking is also enabled
questions.explain: The two postures aren't strictly either/or in practice; they can coexist with a plan to close the public path later.
